answers.answer: !pause pauses music. A moderator or someone the broadcaster granted the right to moderate the song queue can use it, subject to the command’s configured access and a configured music feature. An ordinary viewer without that right is refused. Default normal cooldowns are 30 seconds for chat and 0 seconds per person. Platform-identified broadcasters and moderators bypass normal waits; a bot-stored role alone does not.

Default effective access includes a command’s own safeguards.
For example, !pause needs a moderator or someone granted the right to moderate the music queue, even though its base role in the editor is Everyone.
For music controls, Moderators includes someone the broadcaster granted the right to moderate the song queue.
That gate applies to !pause, !resume, setting !volume, !bansong, !closequeue, !openqueue and !clearsongs.
An ordinary viewer without that right receives a refusal.
The broadcaster and moderators identified on the incoming platform message bypass these normal waits.
A role stored only in the bot does not grant that bypass, and the extra moderator skip window described below still applies.

answers.answer: No. The catalog does not connect a music player; the underlying music feature must be configured. Manage it under Commands then System commands. By default Moderator, Lead moderator, Editor and Broadcaster can change commands, but the broadcaster can raise that requirement. Read-only access does not show the tab. Choose Customize to unlock supported fields, then Save changes.
quote: Music and economy commands need their underlying feature configured.
Having !pause in the catalog does not connect a music player.
To manage a built-in, open Commands, then System commands.
By default, Moderator, Lead moderator, Editor and Broadcaster can change commands; the broadcaster can raise the required role.
Read-only access does not show this tab.
Choose Customize to unlock the supported fields.
Change what you need and choose Save changes.

answers.answer: Choose Back to default beneath the changed cooldown field. It saves immediately without Save changes, and the field shows Using the default. Reset to default is broader: choose it in the footer and confirm in its dialog to lose saved edits, restore both cooldowns, role and all reply wording, switch Read it aloud off, and switch the command back on. Shared wording is restored for the paired command too, but its other settings remain its own.
quote: Choose Back to default beneath a changed field.
It saves immediately, without another Save changes, and the field returns to Using the default.
A reset loses the command’s saved edits and switches it back on.
If it shares replies with another command, the reset also restores that shared wording.
The other command keeps its own enabled state, role, cooldowns and Read it aloud setting.
Open the command and choose Reset to default in the footer.
Read “Reset !name to its default?” and the list of settings that will be lost.
Choose Reset to default in the dialog.
The fields show their defaults and the command is switched on.
Restores the default chat cooldown.
Restores the default per-person cooldown.
Restores the default role.
Restores the default words of every reply.
Switches Read it aloud off.
Enables the command again.

answers.answer: No. After the first successful moderated bare !skip, a separate 30-second channel-wide moderator skip window prevents another moderator skipping five seconds later even though normal cooldowns are bypassed. An ordinary viewer can use !skip 4 to remove their own fourth pending request, counted only among their own queued requests; it does not skip the playing song and normal access/availability checks still apply.
quote: Bare !skip lets a viewer skip only their own currently playing request.
A moderator or music-right holder can skip any playing song, but a successful moderated skip starts a separate 30-second wait for the whole channel.
Another moderator cannot skip again five seconds later, even though moderators bypass normal cooldowns.
A numbered command such as !skip 4 instead removes the caller’s fourth pending request, counting only their own requests in queue order.
It leaves the playing song alone and still requires the command’s normal access checks.
